segments.html:
An attribution graph is a picture of why a model said what it said, drawn in terms of interpretable features rather than layers and heads. This tutorial builds one end to end in NNsight: we take Llama-3.2-1B, replace every MLP with a cross-layer transcoder, verify that the replacement is faithful, trace the graph for a single prompt, check that it is an exact decomposition, and finally test it — by ablating the features the graph blames and watching the answer collapse.

Everything here runs locally on one GPU in about 7 GB.

Why replace the MLPs at all?

Activation patching and attribution patching (our causal mediation tutorials) tell you which layer and position mattered. That is a coordinate, not an explanation. The reason they stop there is that an MLP's hidden units are dense and polysemantic — there is no natural set of "things this MLP did" to attribute to.

A transcoder manufactures that set. It is a dictionary trained to imitate an MLP: it reads the MLP's input, encodes it into a large sparse set of feature activations, and decodes those features back into the MLP's output. Note the asymmetry with an SAE — an SAE reconstructs its own input, so its features describe a representation. A transcoder maps input to output, so its features describe a computation. Its decoder rows are the vectors the MLP writes into the residual stream, one per feature, and on a given prompt only about a dozen per layer and position are non-zero.

A cross-layer transcoder (CLT) goes one step further. A feature born at layer l owns a decoder row for every target layer l,l+1,…,L−1, so a single feature can write into the whole rest of the network. The reconstruction of layer t's MLP output is

mlp_out​t​=btdec​+l≤t∑​f∑​al,f​Wl,fdec​[t−l]

where al,f​ is feature f's activation at layer l. This is the object Anthropic's Circuit Tracing work uses, and it is the reason a feature in the graph is not tied to one layer.

What the graph is a graph of

Swap each MLP for its reconstruction and you get a replacement model. Add back the residual εt​=mlp_outt​−mlp_out​t​ as a frozen constant and you get a local replacement model: numerically identical to the original on this prompt, but now written entirely in terms of quantities you can name. The nodes of the attribution graph are exactly those quantities:

node type one per what it means
feature (layer, position, feature id) with a>0 a dictionary feature that fired
error (layer, position) what the dictionary failed to explain at that site
token position the embedding that entered the stream
logit the target the thing we are explaining

Error nodes are not decoration. They are the honesty mechanism: if your dictionary is bad, the graph will say so by routing the explanation through error nodes instead of features.

An edge i→j is the direct linear effect of node i's value on node j's value — the effect that does not pass through any other feature. We get it by making every node value an autograd leaf and reading xi​⋅∂xj​/∂xi​. For that number to be a direct effect and not a total one, we freeze the two non-linearities that route information between positions and rescale it: attention patterns and LayerNorm scales. With those frozen, the model is linear in every leaf, and by Euler's identity the edges into a node must sum exactly to that node. That is a hard test, and we run it.

Setup

Two warnings before you press run:

  • This notebook needs a local GPU and ~20 GB of free disk. The CLT checkpoint is 20 GB (its decoder alone is 9.1 B parameters). It does not fit in a free Colab session, and unlike the rest of our tutorials it is not written to. We keep GPU usage under 7 GB by leaving the decoder memory-mapped on disk and gathering only the rows for features that actually fired.
  • The task= argument to TransformersModel is not optional here. Without it, loading fails outright when the HuggingFace hub is in offline mode.

Executing the whole notebook takes roughly an hour, almost all of it in section 1's mispaired-dictionary control, which fires 50x more features than the real thing and therefore gathers 50x more decoder rows off disk. The attribution itself takes seconds.

1. Pairing the artifact to the model, numerically

This is the step people skip. A dictionary trained for a different model, a different layer, or a different hook point will still load, still produce sparse features, and still yield a reconstruction that looks like an activation. Every downstream number will be plausible and wrong. So before interpreting anything we establish the pairing from the artifact itself, then confirm it with a number.

The whole specification of mntss/clt-llama-3.2-1b-524k is a four-line config.yaml plus the tensor shapes.

segments.html:
Three things fall out of that:

  • threshold_{l} next to W_enc_{l} means the activation is JumpReLU: a=z⋅1[z>θ], not ReLU. Using ReLU here would silently change the feature set.
  • 32768 features per layer × 16 layers = 524288 total. The "524k" in the name is the total, not the per-layer width — an easy thing to get wrong when you allocate buffers.
  • W_dec_{l} has shape [32768, 16-l, 2048]. The middle axis is the target layer. That second dimension shrinking as l grows is the confirmation that this is genuinely cross-layer: a feature born at layer 3 writes into 13 layers, a feature born at layer 15 into one.

The two hook names are written in TransformerLens vocabulary, and translating them to HuggingFace module paths is a step you have to do by hand:

TransformerLens what it is NNsight path
hook_resid_mid residual after the attention add, before the second LayerNorm model.model.layers[l].post_attention_layernorm.input
hook_mlp_out MLP output, before the residual add model.model.layers[l].mlp.output

Both are bare tensors on transformers 5.x, not tuples. No [0] indexing at either site.

The CLT itself

A small nn.Module. The only design decision worth explaining is dec_rows: the decoder is 18.3 GB in bfloat16, so we never load it. safe_open memory-maps the file, and fancy-indexing the mapped tensor pulls only the rows we ask for — a few hundred features instead of 32768. Keep the file handles alive for as long as you use the mapping.

segments.code:
class CrossLayerTranscoder(torch.nn.Module):
    '''mntss/clt-llama-3.2-1b-524k. Encoders resident (or streamed); decoder mmapped.'''

    def __init__(self, path, device=DEVICE, dtype=torch.bfloat16, n_layers=N_LAYERS,
                 lazy_encoder=True):
        super().__init__()
        self.path, self.dev, self.dtype, self.L = path, device, dtype, n_layers
        self.lazy_encoder = lazy_encoder
        W, b_enc, b_dec, thr = [], [], [], []
        for l in range(n_layers):
            with safe_open(os.path.join(path, f"W_enc_{l}.safetensors"), framework="pt",
                           device=str(device)) as f:
                W.append(f.get_tensor(f"W_enc_{l}").to(dtype))
                b_enc.append(f.get_tensor(f"b_enc_{l}").to(dtype))
                b_dec.append(f.get_tensor(f"b_dec_{l}").to(dtype))
                thr.append(f.get_tensor(f"threshold_{l}").to(dtype))
        self.F, self.D = W[0].shape
        # The encoder is 2.1 GB in bf16. Streaming it off disk one layer at a time keeps us
        # inside the 7 GB budget alongside an fp32 model.
        self.W_enc = None if lazy_encoder else torch.stack(W)
        del W
        self.b_enc, self.b_dec = torch.stack(b_enc), torch.stack(b_dec)
        self.threshold = torch.stack(thr)
        # mmap the 18.3 GB decoder; the handles must stay alive for the mapping to stay valid.
        self._handles = [safe_open(os.path.join(path, f"W_dec_{l}.safetensors"),
                                   framework="pt", device="cpu") for l in range(n_layers)]
        self.W_dec_cpu = [self._handles[l].get_tensor(f"W_dec_{l}") for l in range(n_layers)]

    def _enc_w(self, l):
        if self.W_enc is not None:
            return self.W_enc[l]
        with safe_open(os.path.join(self.path, f"W_enc_{l}.safetensors"), framework="pt",
                       device=str(self.dev)) as f:
            return f.get_tensor(f"W_enc_{l}").to(self.dtype)

    def encode_layer(self, x, l):
        '''JumpReLU encode of resid_mid at layer l -> [..., F].'''
        z = x @ self._enc_w(l).T + self.b_enc[l]
        return z * (z > self.threshold[l])

    def enc_rows(self, l, feat_ids):
        '''Encoder rows for specific features -> [n, D]. Used to define feature targets.'''
        if self.W_enc is not None:
            return self.W_enc[l][feat_ids]
        with safe_open(os.path.join(self.path, f"W_enc_{l}.safetensors"), framework="pt",
                       device="cpu") as f:
            return f.get_slice(f"W_enc_{l}")[feat_ids.cpu()].to(self.dev, self.dtype)

    def dec_rows(self, l, feat_ids):
        '''Decoder rows for features born at layer l -> [n, L-l, D], gathered off the mmap.'''
        if len(feat_ids) == 0:
            return torch.zeros(0, self.L - l, self.D, device=self.dev, dtype=self.dtype)
        return self.W_dec_cpu[l][feat_ids.cpu()].to(self.dev, self.dtype)

Reading both hook points in one trace

We need resid_mid and mlp_out at all 16 layers. The idiom you will see elsewhere in our docs is a list comprehension over layers:

segments.code: resid_mid = nnsight.save([model.model.layers[l].post_attention_layernorm.input for l in range(16)])

segments.html:
That works for one hook point. It breaks for two: a comprehension walks layers 0..15 before the next one starts, so the second comprehension asks for layer 0 after the model has already run to layer 15, and you get OutOfOrderError. With more than one hook point, use a single loop that appends them in forward order.

We also wrap the capture in torch.no_grad(). Read-only traces run with autograd on by default, which here would cost roughly an order of magnitude in memory for nothing.

segments.code:
PROMPT = "The Eiffel Tower is in the city of"
ANSWER = " Paris"

ids = tokenizer(PROMPT, return_tensors="pt")["input_ids"].to(DEVICE)
ans_id = tokenizer(ANSWER, add_special_tokens=False)["input_ids"][0]
toks = [tokenizer.decode([i]) for i in ids[0]]
N_POS = ids.shape[1]
print(toks, "->", repr(ANSWER), ans_id)


def capture(ids):
    '''resid_mid, mlp_out and resid_pre at every layer, plus clean logits. One forward pass.'''
    with torch.no_grad():
        with model.trace(ids):
            resid_pre, resid_mid, mlp_out = nnsight.save([]), nnsight.save([]), nnsight.save([])
            for l in range(N_LAYERS):                       # single loop, forward order
                resid_pre.append(model.model.layers[l].input_layernorm.input.detach())
                resid_mid.append(model.model.layers[l].post_attention_layernorm.input.detach())
                mlp_out.append(model.model.layers[l].mlp.output.detach())
            logits = model.output.logits.detach().save()
    stack = lambda xs: torch.stack([x[0] for x in xs]).float()   # [L, P, D]
    return stack(resid_pre), stack(resid_mid), stack(mlp_out), logits


RP, RM, MO, clean_logits = capture(ids)
print("resid_mid", tuple(RM.shape), " mlp_out", tuple(MO.shape))
print("clean p(%r) = %.4f" % (ANSWER, float(clean_logits[0, -1].softmax(-1)[ans_id])))

segments.html:
Now the actual pairing check. We encode resid_mid, decode into every target layer, and measure the fraction of variance unexplained of mlp_out. Then we run the same measurement two ways that a mispaired artifact would produce:

  1. wrong hook point — encode resid_pre (one module earlier) instead of resid_mid;
  2. wrong layer alignment — score the correct reconstruction against layer t+1's mlp_out.

If the correct pairing does not clearly beat both, you do not have the right artifact.

segments.code:
CHUNK = 4096      # cap the gathered decoder block; a mispaired dictionary can fire 100x more

def reconstruct(feats):
    '''CLT reconstruction of mlp_out at every layer, from a [L, P, F] feature tensor.'''
    P = feats.shape[1]
    recon = clt.b_dec[:, None, :].expand(N_LAYERS, P, clt.D).clone().float()
    for l in range(N_LAYERS):
        nz = (feats[l] > 0).nonzero()                      # [n, 2] = (position, feature)
        if nz.numel() == 0:
            continue
        # scatter-add each feature's contribution into target layers l..L-1 at its own position
        flat = torch.zeros((N_LAYERS - l) * P, clt.D, device=DEVICE)
        tgt_l = torch.arange(N_LAYERS - l, device=DEVICE)
        for c in range(0, nz.shape[0], CHUNK):
            pos, fid = nz[c:c + CHUNK, 0], nz[c:c + CHUNK, 1]
            uniq, inv = fid.unique(return_inverse=True)     # gather each row off the mmap once
            dec = clt.dec_rows(l, uniq)[inv].float()        # [n, L-l, D]
            contrib = dec * feats[l][pos, fid][:, None, None]
            tgt = tgt_l[None, :].expand(len(pos), -1).reshape(-1)
            pp = pos[:, None].expand(-1, N_LAYERS - l).reshape(-1)
            flat.index_add_(0, tgt * P + pp, contrib.reshape(-1, clt.D))
            del dec, contrib
        recon[l:] += flat.reshape(N_LAYERS - l, P, clt.D)
    return recon


def fvu(recon, target, from_pos=1):
    e = (target - recon)[:, from_pos:]
    t = target[:, from_pos:]
    return float(e.pow(2).sum() / (t - t.mean(1, keepdim=True)).pow(2).sum())


def encode_all(stream):
    return torch.stack([clt.encode_layer(stream[l].to(clt.dtype), l).float()
                        for l in range(N_LAYERS)])


t0 = time.time()
feats_correct = encode_all(RM)
feats_wronghook = encode_all(RP)
recon_correct = reconstruct(feats_correct)
recon_wronghook = reconstruct(feats_wronghook)
print("(%.0fs -- the mispaired run dominates: it fires ~50x more features to gather)\n"
      % (time.time() - t0))

def l0(f):
    return float((f > 0).float().sum(-1)[:, 1:].mean())

print("                                              %8s %8s" % ("mean L0", "FVU"))
print("correct pairing  (resid_mid -> mlp_out)       %8.1f %8.4f"
      % (l0(feats_correct), fvu(recon_correct, MO)))
print("wrong hook point (resid_pre -> mlp_out)       %8.1f %8.4f"
      % (l0(feats_wronghook), fvu(recon_wronghook, MO)))
print("wrong layer      (recon_t   -> mlp_out_t+1)   %8s %8.4f"
      % ("-", fvu(recon_correct[:-1], MO[1:])))

del recon_wronghook, feats_wronghook, RP
torch.cuda.empty_cache()
torch.cuda.reset_peak_memory_stats()

FVU 0.21 for the stated pairing: it accounts for 79% of the variance of every MLP output in the model. Both controls are not merely worse — they are worse than predicting the mean, which is what FVU 1.0 means. Reading one module too early scores 215; scoring against the neighbouring layer scores 3.3. A mispaired dictionary does not degrade gracefully.

The L0 column is the second tell, and it is the one you would notice first in practice. Reading one module too early makes the encoder wildly out of distribution, so instead of ~12 features per position it fires hundreds — the input is not the kind of vector the dictionary was trained on, and JumpReLU has no way to say so. That run still produced a full-shaped reconstruction and a plausible sparse code. Nothing errored. Only the numbers tell you.

A residual FVU of 0.21 is also the honest headline: this dictionary does not explain a fifth of what the MLPs do, and that fifth is what error nodes will carry.

2. The BOS trap

Before we splice anything, a caveat that will otherwise cost you an afternoon.

Llama- and Gemma-family models write an enormous attention sink vector into the BOS position. Every position in the model attends to it, and its magnitude has nothing to do with its content. No dictionary is trained on it — by universal convention transcoder features are zeroed at position 0 (circuit_tracer hard-codes zero_positions=slice(0, 1)). So the CLT's reconstruction at position 0 is garbage, and splicing it deletes the sink.

The residual norm at BOS runs 0.8 → 36 → 420 and stays there; everywhere else it is under 20. MLP-0 and MLP-1 are what write it. And the CLT is completely out of distribution there: L0 in the thousands where it is ~12 elsewhere, with activations up to ~1000 against ~5.

Now the consequence. We compare splicing all positions against splicing from position 1, leaving the model's true mlp_out at BOS.

segments.code:
clean_lp = clean_logits[0, -1].log_softmax(-1)

def splice_and_read(recon, from_pos):
    with torch.no_grad():
        with model.trace(ids):
            for l in range(N_LAYERS):
                model.model.layers[l].mlp.output[:, from_pos:] = recon[l][None][:, from_pos:]
            lg = model.output.logits.detach().save()
    lp = lg[0, -1].log_softmax(-1)
    kl = float((clean_lp.exp() * (clean_lp - lp)).sum())
    return float(lp[ans_id].exp()), tokenizer.decode([int(lp.argmax())]), kl


feats_zerobos = feats_correct.clone(); feats_zerobos[:, 0] = 0
recon_zerobos = reconstruct(feats_zerobos)

with torch.no_grad():
    with model.trace(ids):
        for l in range(N_LAYERS):
            model.model.layers[l].mlp.output[:] = 0.0
        zero_lg = model.output.logits.detach().save()
zero_lp = zero_lg[0, -1].log_softmax(-1)

rows = [
    ("zero BOS features, splice ALL positions",  splice_and_read(recon_zerobos, 0)),
    ("keep BOS features, splice ALL positions",  splice_and_read(recon_correct, 0)),
    ("zero BOS features, splice from position 1", splice_and_read(recon_zerobos, 1)),

3. The replacement-model anchor

A replacement model that does not reproduce the model's behaviour is not a replacement model. Everything downstream is conditional on this number, so we measure it properly: next-token cross-entropy on held-out text, not the answer probability of the one prompt we care about.

Three conditions, and the two that bracket the answer matter as much as the one we want:

  • clean — the real model, the floor;
  • CLT replacement — every mlp_out replaced by the reconstruction, positions ≥ 1;
  • mlp_out := 0 — the MLPs deleted, the ceiling.

The statistic is the fraction of the clean→ablated gap the replacement recovers. We add mlp_out := b_dec as a fourth line, which is the CLT with all features off: it separates "the features are doing the work" from "the decoder bias happens to be a good constant".

def next_token_ce(logits, ids, from_pos=1):
    lp = logits[0, :-1].float().log_softmax(-1)
    tgt = ids[0, 1:]
    keep = torch.arange(len(tgt), device=ids.device) >= (from_pos - 1)

def splice_ce(t_ids, fn):
    with torch.no_grad():
        with model.trace(t_ids):
            for l in range(N_LAYERS):

            lg = model.output.logits.detach().save()
    return next_token_ce(lg, t_ids)

4. The local replacement model

To attribute, we need something stronger than a faithful replacement: we need an exact one whose every ingredient is an autograd leaf.

The construction is one line of arithmetic. For each layer t,

mlp_outt​:=function of the leaf amlp_out​t​(a)​​+leaf constant εt​(mlp_outt​−mlp_out​t​(a)).detach()​​

Numerically this is the identity — the forward pass is bit-for-bit the original model. But a, the vector of active feature activations, is now a leaf tensor built outside the trace, and torch.autograd.grad on it returns ∂(anything)/∂as​ for all ~2000 features in one backward pass. The CLT's several per-target-layer decoder rows for a feature are accumulated into one gradient by autograd, which is why the cross-layer case needs no extra code over the single-layer case.

An edge is supposed to be a direct effect. Left alone, changing feature s would also change where attention looks and how LayerNorm rescales — paths that are not "feature s writes into feature t's input". Anthropic's formulation freezes both, and so do we.

Neither is exposed as a module output, so we reach inside the forward with .source. Printing it renders the actual HuggingFace source with a handle on every operation.

def build_leaves(ids, dtype=torch.float32):
    '''Clean pass -> active features, their encoder/decoder rows, and the error term.'''
    P = ids.shape[1]
    _, rm, mo, clean = capture(ids)

    feats = encode_all(rm)
    feats[:, 0] = 0                                   # BOS: the CLT is out of distribution there

    nz = (feats > 0).nonzero()                        # [S, 3] = (layer, position, feature)
    s_layer, s_pos, s_feat = nz[:, 0], nz[:, 1], nz[:, 2]
    S = nz.shape[0]
    a_vals = feats[s_layer, s_pos, s_feat].clone()    # [S]

    # Per-active-feature encoder row (defines its own target) and decoder rows padded to
    # [S, L, D] so that feature s born at layer l writes into target layers l..L-1.
    dec = torch.zeros(S, N_LAYERS, clt.D, device=DEVICE)
    enc = torch.zeros(S, clt.D, device=DEVICE)
    for l in range(N_LAYERS):
        m = s_layer == l
        if not m.any():
            continue
        uniq, inv = s_feat[m].unique(return_inverse=True)
        dec[m, l:, :] = clt.dec_rows(l, uniq)[inv].float()
        enc[m] = clt.enc_rows(l, uniq)[inv].float()
    return dict(P=P, S=S, MO=mo, feats=feats, clean=clean, a_vals=a_vals, dec=dec, enc=enc,
                s_layer=s_layer, s_pos=s_pos, s_feat=s_feat)


def recon_from_a(st, a, bias):
    '''Differentiable CLT reconstruction of every mlp_out from the leaf `a`. -> [L, P, D]'''
    S, P = st["S"], st["P"]
    contrib = a[:, None, None] * st["dec"]                              # [S, L, D]
    tgt = torch.arange(N_LAYERS, device=a.device)[None, :].expand(S, -1).reshape(-1)
    pp = st["s_pos"][:, None].expand(-1, N_LAYERS).reshape(-1)
    flat = torch.zeros(N_LAYERS * P, clt.D, device=a.device)
    flat = flat.index_add(0, tgt * P + pp, contrib.reshape(-1, clt.D))
    return flat.reshape(N_LAYERS, P, clt.D) + bias[:, None, :]


def local_replacement(st, ids, freeze=True):
    '''One trace. Returns live, graph-carrying tensors: the leaves and the outputs.'''
    a = st["a_vals"].clone().requires_grad_(True)
    # b_dec is a constant the CLT injects at every layer. Making it a leaf too lets the
    # closure check below account for it instead of leaving it as an unexplained remainder.
    bias = clt.b_dec.float().clone().requires_grad_(True)
    recon = recon_from_a(st, a, bias)
    err = (st["MO"] - recon.detach()).clone().requires_grad_(True)      # leaf constant

    with model.trace(ids):
        emb = model.model.embed_tokens.output.detach().requires_grad_(True)
        model.model.embed_tokens.output = emb                           # token nodes
        resid_mid = nnsight.save([])
        for l in range(N_LAYERS):
            if freeze:                                    # strictly forward order
                v = model.model.layers[l].input_layernorm.source.mean_0.output
                model.model.layers[l].input_layernorm.source.mean_0.output = v.detach()
                qk = model.model.layers[l].self_attn.source.apply_rotary_pos_emb_0.output
                model.model.layers[l].self_attn.source.apply_rotary_pos_emb_0.output = \
                    (qk[0].detach(), qk[1].detach())
            resid_mid.append(model.model.layers[l].post_attention_layernorm.input)
            if freeze:
                v2 = model.model.layers[l].post_attention_layernorm.source.mean_0.output
                model.model.layers[l].post_attention_layernorm.source.mean_0.output = v2.detach()
            model.model.layers[l].mlp.output = (recon[l] + err[l])[None]
        if freeze:
            vn = model.model.norm.source.mean_0.output
            model.model.norm.source.mean_0.output = vn.detach()
        logits = model.output.logits.save()
        resid_mid = nnsight.save(resid_mid)
        emb = nnsight.save(emb)
    return dict(a=a, err=err, emb=emb, bias=bias, resid_mid=resid_mid, logits=logits)

5. Edges, and the closure check

The target. Following circuit_tracer, we explain the demeaned answer logit — the answer logit minus the mean over the top-k logits — because a direction that raises all logits equally changes nothing about the model's prediction.

The demeaning convention is easy to get subtly wrong and it does not announce itself. An attribution graph built with the wrong target direction still has sensible sparse rows, sensible magnitudes, and an interpretable-looking top-10. Fix the convention before you interpret.

One backward gives the whole logit row at once: every feature edge, every error edge, every token edge.

The full adjacency: one backward per node

Every node needs its own row. A feature node's value is its activation, which by construction is the encoder row dotted into resid_mid at that layer and position — a scalar we can differentiate just like the logit. So the graph is 1947 backward passes through a 1B model.

We expected this to be the hard part. It is not: torch.autograd.grad with retain_graph=True reuses the single forward graph we already built, and returns gradients rather than accumulating into .grad, so there is no zeroing between calls and nothing to .save().

NNsight also offers with target.backward(): leaf.grad.save(), documented for exactly this "backward outside a forward trace" pattern, and it gives bit-identical results here. We use torch.autograd.grad for the loop only because it avoids per-call bookkeeping.

The one thing to watch is that the per-call cost grows with how deep the target sits — the graph below a layer-15 target is 16x the graph below a layer-0 target.

7. The causal anchor

Everything so far is a decomposition. A decomposition can be exact and still not tell you anything useful about what the model needs — it is a statement about gradients, not about counterfactuals. So we test it.

The experiment. Take the top-K features the graph blames, subtract their CLT contribution from mlp_out at their own position for every layer they write into, and read p(" Paris"). Do it on the real model, with attention and LayerNorm live and the error terms untouched — not on the replacement.

The controls, which are the actual argument. A dramatic collapse means nothing on its own, because ablating almost anything from a model hurts it. We need to know that attribution picked the features, and not something a much simpler heuristic would have found:

  1. top-K by |activation| — the features that fired hardest. If this works as well, you never needed a graph.
  2. random features matched on activation — same magnitudes, no attribution, 5 draws.
  3. uniform random features — the floor.

def ablate(idx):
    '''Subtract the CLT contribution of the listed features from mlp_out, on the REAL model.'''
    delta = torch.zeros(N_LAYERS, P, clt.D, device=DEVICE)
    if len(idx):
        idx = torch.as_tensor(list(idx), device=DEVICE)
        contrib = st["a_vals"][idx][:, None, None] * dec[idx]           # [n, L, D]
        n = len(idx)
        tgt = torch.arange(N_LAYERS, device=DEVICE)[None, :].expand(n, -1).reshape(-1)
        pp = s_pos_d[idx][:, None].expand(-1, N_LAYERS).reshape(-1)
        flat = torch.zeros(N_LAYERS * P, clt.D, device=DEVICE)
        flat.index_add_(0, tgt * P + pp, contrib.reshape(-1, clt.D))
        delta = flat.reshape(N_LAYERS, P, clt.D)
    with torch.no_grad():
        with model.trace(ids):
            for l in range(N_LAYERS):
                model.model.layers[l].mlp.output = model.model.layers[l].mlp.output - delta[l][None]
            lg = model.output.logits.detach().save()
    lg = lg[0, -1]
    return float(lg.softmax(-1)[ans_id]), tokenizer.decode([int(lg.argmax())])

8. Comparison with circuit-tracer

Anthropic's circuit-tracer is the reference implementation of this method, and it has an NNsight backend.

The numbers in this section come from a separate cross-check, not from a cell above: circuit_tracer needs its own environment and is deliberately not a dependency of this notebook. We ran its attribute_nnsight on the identical prompt and aligned the common feature nodes. It finds 1951 active features to our 1947 (the four extra sit within float noise of the JumpReLU threshold), and across the 3.79 M feature→feature edges the two adjacency matrices agree to Pearson 0.999963 / Spearman 1.000000, with an identical top-10 by direct attribution. Since the two implementations differ in almost every choice below the method, that agreement is the strongest evidence either is right.

Where they differ:

this notebook circuit-tracer
attention freeze detach q, k at self_attn.source.apply_rotary_pos_emb_0 detach post-softmax probabilities
backward organisation leaf tensors + one torch.autograd.grad per target replicate the prompt into a batch of 512, inject custom gradients
CLT bookkeeping autograd accumulates a feature's per-target-layer decoder rows explicit encoder_to_decoder_map / decoder_locations
forward pass genuinely spliced (so it can be evaluated as a replacement model) out = skip + (out - skip).detach(), numerically the identity
peak memory 7.1 GB 10.8 GB

Wall clock was a wash in the head-to-head (7.9 s against 8.3 s to build the full adjacency), and both are contention-dependent on a shared card, so the memory column is the one to read.

Two of these are worth pulling out.

The leaf formulation removes a bookkeeping layer. Because a is a leaf and the reconstruction is an ordinary differentiable function of it, autograd sums a cross-layer feature's contributions across all the layers it writes into, for free. The CLT case needs no code the single-layer case does not.

circuit-tracer deletes the BOS error node. setup_attribution runs error_vectors[:, zero_positions] = 0, so every position-0 error edge is exactly zero. Zeroing the BOS features is correct — the encoder is hopelessly out of distribution there. Zeroing the BOS error on top of that throws the residual away instead of accounting for it. On this prompt the layer-1 BOS error edge alone is +0.73 of a 5.58 target — 13%, and exactly the attention-sink write we measured in section 2. It is also why their decomposition does not close and ours does.

Where NNsight helped, and where it did not

.source is what made this tractable. Printing model.model.layers[0].self_attn.source renders HuggingFace's actual forward with a handle on every operation, so finding a freeze point took a minute of reading rather than a monkeypatch of LlamaAttention.forward. It also let us pick a different freeze point from the reference, and the two agree.

Three places it was harder than it needed to be:

  • Two hook points need one interleaved loop. The list-comprehension idiom you will find throughout our docs works for one hook point and raises OutOfOrderError for two. The same rule applies to .source sites, which must be requested in forward order relative to everything else.
  • OutOfOrderError names what you asked for but not where the model actually is. When we ordered the self_attn freeze before the input_layernorm freeze, the message named the module correctly and we still misdiagnosed it.
  • There is no batched-VJP helper. The natural way to ask for 300 attribution rows at once is torch.autograd.grad(..., is_grads_batched=True), which does not compose with a traced forward. A tracer.vjp(tensor, directions) that batches the backward without batching the forward would beat both our loop and circuit-tracer's prompt replication.

Limitations

The replacement model is not the model. It recovers 94.4% of the next-token loss gap and it keeps the answer on this prompt, but on the Texas prompt p(" Austin") falls from 0.974 to 0.003. Aggregate faithfulness does not imply per-prompt faithfulness, and an attribution graph is a per-prompt object. Check your specific prompt before you interpret its graph.

One prompt, one model, one dictionary. Everything here is a single forward pass of Llama-3.2-1B. Nothing generalises to the prompt you have not run, and a feature that is load-bearing here may be inert one paraphrase away. The 'iff' finding in particular is about how this tokenizer splits "Eiffel".

Freezing is an assumption, not a fact. Freezing attention and LayerNorm is what makes the decomposition exact, but it also defines what "direct effect" means. The paths we froze — a feature changing where attention looks — are real paths in the real model, and the graph is silent about them by construction. The unfrozen closure residual of 8.77 is a lower bound on how much the graph is choosing not to see.

FVU 0.21 is not small. A fifth of what the MLPs do is not described by any feature. On this prompt that fifth turns out to be mostly orthogonal to the answer direction (error nodes carry 5.3%), but that is a property of this prompt, not a guarantee — on the Texas prompt it is 27%.

We did not interpret the features. We have shown that feature #9970 at layer 2 is causally necessary for the answer; we have not shown what it means. That needs max-activating examples or auto-interpretation over a corpus, and without it a graph tells you the shape of a computation rather than its content.

No ablation is neutral. We subtract a feature's contribution, which is a zero-ablation of that feature — known to overstate importance relative to mean- or resample-ablation. The controls are what make the comparison fair: every arm of the sweep uses the identical ablation, so the gap between influence-ranked and activation-ranked features cannot be an artifact of the ablation choice.
